pamphlet_excerpts: Focusing on Personal Abilities: Many people with disabilities want to emphasize what they are able to do rather than emphasize their disabilities (p. 9).
Recognizing the Person First: Remember that people with disabilities are people first (p. 9).
Respecting Individual Self-Description: Each person gets to decide how he or she should be described (p. 9).
Applying Person-First Language: You should use person-first language when talking about people who are not personal acquaintances or about people with disabilities as a group (p. 9).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Honor Personal Description Choices: Each person gets to decide how he or she should be described (p. 9).
Step 2 - Use Person-First Language: You should use person-first language when talking about people who are not personal acquaintances or about people with disabilities as a group (p. 9).
Step 3 - Ask New Friends Directly: When you make a new friend or talk about an individual, show a person-first attitude by calling the individual what he orshe wants to be called (p. 9).
Step 4 - Acknowledge Whole Personal Identity: Many people with disabilities see their condition as part of who they are, just like their gender, hair or eye color, or ethnicity (p. 9).

options: A. Speak only to the person's companion or interpreter in a loud voice, and assume anyone who does not use a wheelchair has no disability.
B. Push a person's wheelchair or grab a blind person's white cane without asking so you can move them through doorways faster.

C. Speak directly to the individual using respectful people-first or preferred language, ask before offering physical assistance, and recognize that many disabilities (such as autism, epilepsy, diabetes, hearing loss, or learning differences) are not immediately visible.
D. Avoid inviting Scouts with physical or sensory disabilities on campouts so the troop does not have to adjust trail plans.

pamphlet_excerpts: Early Career Preparation: If a career in audiology interests you, you should begin early to get the background needed (p. 19).
Foundational High School Courses: In school, take biology, physical science, language, and physical education classes (p. 19).
Agency Volunteering and Employment: Get an after-schooljob or volunteer with an agency or organization that serves people who have disabilities (p. 19).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Volunteer With Support Agencies: Get an after-schooljob or volunteer with an agency or organization that serves people who have disabilities (p. 19).
Step 2 - Observe Professional Hearing Diagnoses: Audiologists are trained to detect and diagnose hearing problems (p. 19).
Step 3 - Measure Hearing With Audio meters: An audiologist uses an instrument called anaudiometer to test a person's hearing (p. 19).
Step 4 - Conduct Behavioral Sound Assessments: An audiologist also may give behavioral tests to find out how a person reacts to various sounds and vibrations (p. 19).

options: A. Speak only to the person's companion or interpreter in a loud voice, and assume anyone who does not use a wheelchair has no disability.
B. Push a person's wheelchair or grab a blind person's white cane without asking so you can move them through doorways faster.
